title: Color and I Are One: from the Bern music house to Kairouan and the angel of history
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Münchenbuchsee, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a village ten kilometres north of Bern a son is born to Hans Klee, a German music teacher out of Franconia, and Ida Frick, a Swiss singer trained at Stuttgart. The child takes his father's German citizenship and will carry it for sixty years, in Switzerland, in Germany, and in the German army. The father teaches music and the mother sings it. The boy is handed a violin before he is handed a pencil. The family stays in Münchenbuchsee barely a year. Bern will hold him for the whole of his childhood and again for the whole of his end.
suggested_refs: Parish register of Münchenbuchsee, Canton Bern, 18 December 1879

stops.name: Bern, the family settles and the violin begins
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted; city-centre pin, no street address established
stops.campa: The Klees move into Bern and the boy grows up in a city that expects a musician of him. He begins violin at the municipal music school around his seventh year, plays well enough by eleven to be taken on as an extraordinary member of the Bern Music Association, and fills the margins of his schoolbooks with drawings his teachers do not encourage. His grandmother gives him coloured chalks. He will decide against the violin on the grounds that the music of his own century is already finished, and painting is not.
suggested_refs: The Bern municipal music school; the Bernische Musikgesellschaft rolls

stops.name: Bern, the diary opens
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At eighteen he begins a diary and keeps it twenty-one years, through Munich, Italy, Tunisia, and the war, closing it in 1918. His son Felix will edit it for publication decades later, and the extent of that editing is a question Klee scholarship has still not closed. In these first Bern pages he is a gymnasium student who plays Bach in the orchestra pit, draws satirical grotesques, and works out that line is the thing he has. He leaves for Munich the following year.
suggested_refs: The Tagebücher, 1897-1918, in the Felix Klee edition of 1957 and the Kersten critical edition of 1988
sources: The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, UC Press, 1964

stops.name: Munich, Knirr's private school
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted; the pool's chronology lens wrongly placed him at the Academy in this year
stops.campa: Klee arrives in Munich at nineteen and enters the private drawing school of Heinrich Knirr, the standard preparation for the Academy, which has not admitted him. He grinds at the figure for two years. Knirr rates his draughtsmanship high and says nothing about his colour, which does not yet exist. The city he has come to is the German capital of painting, full of ateliers, models, and Secessionists. Klee moves through it as a provincial with a violin case, playing in orchestras for money and drawing all day toward a competence he has no idea how to spend.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Knirr's private art school, Schwabing, Munich

stops.name: Munich, the Academy and Franz von Stuck
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: In October 1900 he is admitted to the painting class of Franz von Stuck at the Academy of Fine Arts, the same class Wassily Kandinsky enters at nearly the same moment. Stuck is the symbolist prince of Munich, maker of dark allegorical machines, and what Klee learns from him is mostly that he does not want to make them. He stays a little over a year. He leaves the Academy with a trained hand and no subject of his own, and no professor in Munich is offering one.
suggested_refs: The Akademie der Bildenden Künste München, Stuck's painting class, matriculation October 1900

stops.name: Milan, the journey south begins
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On 22 October 1901 Klee leaves for Italy with the Swiss sculptor Hermann Haller, entering by Milan. The journey will run seven months and cross Genoa, Livorno, Pisa, Rome, Porto d'Anzio, Naples, Pompeii, Sorrento, Positano, Amalfi, the Gargano, and Florence. He goes as every northern art student goes, to stand in front of originals after years of copying plaster casts, and he goes with the diary open beside him. He comes back without a style and with a measure of the distance between his own work and everything he has just looked at.
suggested_refs: The Italian journey of 22 October 1901 to 2 May 1902, itinerary in de.wikipedia

stops.name: Rome, the Forum and the Vatican
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted; he winters in Rome from November into January
stops.campa: Klee winters in Rome, working through the Forum, the Vatican collections, and the early Christian churches. The diary records the encounter as decisive in a way no Munich studio ever was. He copies little and looks long. Michelangelo overwhelms him. The small anonymous things hold him longer, mosaic, wall scratching, votive scrawl, the work of craftsmen nobody kept the names of, and that appetite for the marginal and the childlike is the one thing from Rome that never leaves him.
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum and the Vatican Museums, winter 1901-1902
sources: The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee

stops.name: Naples, the buried towns
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: The southern leg takes the two Swiss to Naples in January, to the harbour, the aquarium, and the archaeological museum holding what Vesuvius covered. Klee walks the excavated streets of Pompeii, a Roman town stopped mid-sentence and dug out again. He is twenty-two, short of money, and standing in front of wall painting made by hands whose names nobody wrote down. The Amalfi coast follows, Sorrento and Positano and Amalfi under a light that leaves almost no trace in the diary. Rome he writes about at length. The south he simply takes in.
suggested_refs: The Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples; the excavations at Pompeii

stops.name: Florence, the tour closes
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested, day defaulted; return to Switzerland 2 May 1902
stops.campa: The Italian journey ends in Florence and Klee turns north for Bern on 2 May 1902, seven months after Milan. He has seen the Renaissance entire and it has given him no manner to work in, only a standard high enough to make the next four years lean ones. He goes home to his parents' house with no studio, no market, and one stubborn conviction, written into the diary that June: that becoming a particular person is the work, and painting well early is not the work at all.
stops.quote: The main thing now is not to paint precociously but to be, or at least become, an individual.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, diary entry, 3 June 1902, in The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, University of California Press, 1964; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Florence, the closing station of the 1901-1902 Italian journey

stops.name: Bern, the etchings and the blackened glass
stops.date_confidence: the Inventions cycle is dated 1903-1905; month and day defaulted to the range's opening year
stops.campa: Back in his parents' house Klee spends four years without income, playing violin with the Bernische Musikgesellschaft for money and cutting into zinc. Between 1903 and 1905 he produces eleven etchings he calls Inventions, grotesques of thin bodies and long necks, satire pushed until it turns into nightmare. He also blackens panes of glass and scratches images into them with a needle, some fifty-seven works made by taking light away rather than laying paint on. He can draw and cannot yet paint, and the technique suits that exactly.
suggested_refs: The Inventions, eleven zinc-plate etchings, 1903-1905; the blackened-glass panels of 1905

stops.name: Paris, the first look
stops.date_confidence: May-June 1905 attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: In May 1905 Klee makes a short first visit to Paris with two friends, walking the Louvre and the salons and looking at Impressionism at close range. He comes home in June unconverted; Paris has not opened a door for him. In the same year's diary he works out where beauty actually resides, and the answer is not in the thing depicted. Thirty years later the objects in his pictures are arrows, fish, letters, and faces built from six lines and a colour nobody ever saw on a face.
stops.quote: The beautiful, which is perhaps inseparable from art, is not after all tied to the subject, but to the pictorial representation.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, diary entry, December 1905 (#733), in The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, University of California Press, 1964; via Wikiquote. Quoted here in full; the truncated form ending at 'subject' inverts the sense.
suggested_refs: The Louvre and the Paris salons of spring 1905

stops.name: Munich, the marriage to Lily Stumpf
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's chronology lens wrongly placed this wedding in Bern
stops.campa: On 15 September 1906 Klee marries Lily Stumpf, a Bavarian pianist he met in a Munich music circle six years earlier, and the couple settle in Munich. She teaches piano and earns the household its money; he keeps the house, raises the child, and paints in the hours the child leaves him. Felix Paul Klee arrives on 30 November 1907. For a decade the arrangement is the reverse of what Munich expects of a married painter. It buys him the working time no patron is paying for.
suggested_refs: Munich civil marriage record, 15 September 1906

stops.name: Munich, the Schwabing studio
stops.date_confidence: the Feilitzschstrasse 3 tenancy runs 1908-1919; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: From 1908 the Klees live and work at Feilitzschstrasse 3 in Schwabing, the quarter where Munich keeps its painters and its theosophists. Rudolf Steiner is lecturing in this city in these same years to audiences that include Kandinsky, though nothing attests that Klee sits in them. Klee illustrates Voltaire's Candide, studies Cezanne and Van Gogh in the Munich exhibitions, and works small, on paper, in black and white. He is thirty and has not solved colour. He names the problem in the diary and keeps it in front of him.
stops.quote: Nature can afford to be prodigal in everything, the artist must be frugal down to the last detail.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, diary entry, Munich, 1909 (#857), in The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, University of California Press, 1964; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Feilitzschstrasse 3, Schwabing, Munich, the Klee apartment and studio 1908-1919

stops.name: Bern, the first exhibition
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In 1910 Klee holds his first solo exhibition in Bern and it travels on to other Swiss cities. His own city shows him first, ten years after he left it. The Munich dealer Hans Goltz gives him a second show the following year. Nothing sells in quantity and nothing changes materially, but the sheets are on walls and a graphic reputation starts to form around them. He is thirty-one and still living on his wife's piano lessons. Kandinsky and Marc are one year away.
suggested_refs: The 1910 Bern solo exhibition and its Swiss tour; Galerie Hans Goltz, Munich, 1911

stops.name: Munich, Schwabing: the almanac circle
stops.date_confidence: Kubin meeting January 1911 attested; the circle forms across 1911, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In January 1911 Klee meets Alfred Kubin, who sets him to illustrating Candide; by autumn he is inside the circle around Kandinsky and Franz Marc assembling Der Blaue Reiter. Seventeen of his graphic works hang in the group's second exhibition in February 1912. Rudolf von Laban is dissolving movement in these same Schwabing streets, Mary Wigman passes through the city in February 1914, and in Sweden Hilma af Klint has been painting non-objective canvases that nobody in Munich will see for seventy years. The almanac argues that art comes from inner necessity. Klee signs.
suggested_refs: Der Blaue Reiter almanac, Munich 1912; the second Blaue Reiter exhibition, February 1912

stops.name: Paris, Delaunay's studio
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Paris stay runs 2 to 18 April 1912, the Delaunay call on 11 April
stops.campa: Klee returns to Paris for two weeks in April 1912 and this time the city opens. On 11 April he calls on Robert Delaunay and sees the Windows, cubism turned into planes of pure colour with the object nearly gone out of them. He takes Delaunay's essay on light home and translates it into German for Der Sturm. The visit gives him what Munich could not teach: a way of building a picture out of colour relations, rather than drawing a thing first and then filling the drawing in.
suggested_refs: Robert Delaunay, 'La Lumiere', translated by Klee for Der Sturm, 1913

stops.name: Cologne, the Sonderbund
stops.date_confidence: the exhibition runs May to September 1912; day defaulted
stops.campa: Klee goes to Cologne for the Sonderbund exhibition, the largest showing of modern European painting Germany has yet mounted: Van Gogh in force, Cezanne, Munch, Gauguin, Picasso, the Fauves. In one building he sees the whole argument he has joined. Two years later the same generation is scattered by a war that kills August Macke in September 1914 and Franz Marc at Verdun in 1916. For the moment the pictures hang together in Cologne, and the future of European painting looks like a room a man can walk through in an afternoon.
suggested_refs: The Internationale Kunstausstellung des Sonderbundes westdeutscher Kunstfreunde und Künstler, Cologne, 1912

stops.name: Marseille, the embarkation
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia dates the whole journey from 3 April 1914, departing via Lyon and Marseille; no reachable source gives the actual embarkation day, and the '5 April' in circulation is unattested
stops.campa: In the first days of April 1914 Klee travels down through Lyon to Marseille with August Macke and the Swiss painter Louis Moilliet, and the three of them take ship for Tunis. Moilliet has the contacts: a Swiss doctor, Ernst Jaggi, with a house in a garden suburb outside the city. Klee is thirty-four and goes as the least established of the three. Twelve days later he will come back with the one sentence every account of his life quotes, and Macke, the most naturally gifted of them, will have five months left to live.
suggested_refs: The Vieux Port of Marseille, embarkation for Tunis, April 1914

stops.name: Tunis, the medina
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The three land at Tunis on 7 April and walk into the medina, a city built of white cubes and shadow, where the light does not model form so much as cut it out. Klee's diary registers the shock as an ordering rather than as exoticism: the old city is already geometry, already the flat coloured rectangle he has been trying to invent. Gustave Flaubert came to this harbour in April 1858 to look at Carthage for Salammbo. Carl Jung will walk this medina in 1920 and feel Europe fall off him inside it. Klee gets twelve days.
suggested_refs: The medina of Tunis, April 1914; Klee's Tunisian watercolours in the Zentrum Paul Klee

stops.name: Saint-Germain, the garden suburb
stops.date_confidence: itinerary day attested; coordinate corrected to present-day Ezzahra, founded 10 September 1909 as Saint-Germain
stops.campa: The party lodges at Saint-Germain, a French colonial garden suburb south of Tunis founded five years earlier and now called Ezzahra, in the house of Doctor Jaggi. It is the base for the excursions. Klee paints watercolours of villas, gardens, and shuttered walls, working small and fast, laying transparent squares of colour edge to edge and letting the paper carry the light. In the sheets made here the colour is the structure of the picture rather than something applied to it, which is new in his work.
suggested_refs: Ezzahra, formerly Saint-Germain, Ben Arous, Tunisia; the villa of Dr Ernst Jaggi

stops.name: Carthage, the ruins
stops.date_confidence: itinerary day attested
stops.campa: An excursion out to Carthage, where Rome ploughed the Punic city under and then built its own on top of it, leaving cisterns, a hill, and a view across the Gulf of Tunis. Gustave Flaubert stood on this ground in April 1858 taking notes for Salammbo and complained there was nothing left to see. Klee is not looking for the Punic city. He is looking at the way sea, hill, and sky divide the field into three bands of colour, which is precisely what his Tunisian sheets keep doing: horizontal registers, a few signs, no perspective at all.
suggested_refs: The Punic and Roman ruins of Carthage, Byrsa hill

stops.name: Sidi Bou Said, the village on the cliff
stops.date_confidence: itinerary day attested; canonical atlas pin inherited from michel_foucault.journey.json
stops.campa: The white and blue village on the cliff north of Tunis, above the gulf, where all three painters work. Klee's sheets from Sidi Bou Said reduce the houses to leaning quadrangles of ochre, rose, and violet, held together by nothing except their edges. Michel Foucault will rent a house in this village in 1967 and write much of a book in it. Europeans keep reporting the same thing: a painter who copies what is in front of him here arrives at abstraction without having to argue himself into it.
suggested_refs: Sidi Bou Said, Gulf of Tunis; the April 1914 watercolours of Klee, Macke, and Moilliet

stops.name: Hammamet, the walled town
stops.date_confidence: itinerary days 11-12 April attested; a minority of accounts place the famous diary passage here rather than at Kairouan
stops.campa: South down the coast to Hammamet, its medina walled against the sea, gardens of orange and jasmine behind the wall. Klee's watercolours from this town are among the best known of the trip. Some accounts place the famous diary passage here rather than at Kairouan, a few days earlier than the usual date, and Felix Klee's later editing of the diary makes the question impossible now to settle. Within one week on this coast Klee stops drawing pictures and starts building them out of colour.
suggested_refs: The medina of Hammamet; Klee's 'Hammamet mit der Moschee', 1914, Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources: The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee (contested attribution)

stops.name: Kairouan, color and I are one
stops.date_confidence: majority reading; the site and date of diary entry #926 are disputed in the secondary literature, with Hammamet a few days earlier as the alternative, and Felix Klee's editing of the diary unresolved. Canonical atlas Kairouan pin inherited from ziryab.journey.json and dihya.journey.json; the Great Mosque itself stands about 750 m north-east of this point
stops.campa: Inland to Kairouan, the fourth holy city of Islam, where the Great Mosque of Uqba holds the desert light without softening any of it. Here, on or about 16 April 1914, Klee writes the sentence his whole life is afterwards read backwards from: color has taken possession of him, he no longer has to chase after it, color and he are one, he is a painter. Klee is in the town perhaps a day and a half. He leaves it having declared himself, in writing, in the second person of his own diary, a painter.
stops.quote: Color has taken possession of me; no longer do I have to chase after it, I know that it has hold of me forever...Color and I are one. I am a painter.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, diary entry #926, dated Tunisia, 16 April 1914, in The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, University of California Press, 1964; via Wikiquote. Text attested; place and date contested.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Uqba, Kairouan; diary entry #926

stops.name: Naples, the way home
stops.date_confidence: return leg Palermo, Naples, Rome, Milan attested; the specific day is reconstructed from the 22 April close of the Tunisian portion
stops.campa: The return runs Palermo, Naples, Rome, Milan, the reverse of the journey he made as a student thirteen years earlier, through the same port he walked in 1902. He reaches Munich at the end of April. At the end of July Austria declares war on Serbia; on 26 September August Macke is killed at Perthes-les-Hurlus in Champagne, aged twenty-seven, and Klee writes the obituary for the friend who took him to Tunisia. The colour method he brought out of those twelve days runs through the next twenty-six years of work.
suggested_refs: Klee's obituary notice for August Macke, 1914

stops.name: Landshut, the conscription
stops.date_confidence: date attested; Landshut as the training depot is reconstructed, not confirmed in any source reachable here
stops.campa: On 5 March 1916 Klee is called up as a Landsturmsoldat and sent for basic training, the day after Franz Marc is killed at Verdun. He is thirty-six, a German citizen born in Switzerland, and the army finds him a poor soldier and a serviceable clerk. He never sees the front. Macke is two years dead, Marc is one day dead, and Klee will spend the war painting in Bavarian barracks rooms on whatever paper the quartermaster is not counting. The barracks sheets are much of what he shows when the war ends.
stops.quote: The more horrible this world (as today, for instance), the more abstract our art.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, diary entry, 1915 (#951), in The Diaries of Paul Klee 1898-1918, ed. Felix Klee, University of California Press, 1964; via Wikiquote. Written the year before the call-up.
suggested_refs: Bavarian Landsturm records, March 1916

stops.name: Oberschleissheim, the aircraft company
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate corrected from the pool's value, which fell about 4 km away in the Feldmoching outskirts
stops.campa: On 20 August 1916 he is transferred to an aircraft maintenance company at Oberschleissheim outside Munich, where the work is varnishing wings and stencilling numbers onto fuselages. He watches wrecked machines brought in on flatbeds, and he draws them. The angels, birds, arrows, and twittering machines of the later work start here, in a hangar where a conscripted painter handles the wreckage of flight for army wages. He is fed, housed, and out of the line.
suggested_refs: The Schleissheim airfield and its Flieger-Ersatz-Abteilung, 1916

stops.name: Gersthofen, the clerk at the flying school
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On 17 January 1917 Klee is reassigned as a clerk to the paymaster of the Royal Bavarian flying school at Gersthofen near Augsburg, and stays there until the war ends in November 1918. The posting gives him an office, a window, and time. He paints in it steadily and sells out of it: by 1917 German criticism is naming him among the leading figures of the new painting, and his dealer cannot get enough sheets to meet the demand. The war that killed his two closest colleagues is what makes his market.
suggested_refs: Königlich Bayerische Fliegerschule V, Gersthofen, 1917-1918

stops.name: Weimar, the Bauhaus appointment
stops.date_confidence: appointed 29 October 1920, teaching begins 10 January 1921, both attested; the '1922 joining date' flagged in some compilations is a confusion with Kandinsky. Canonical atlas Weimar Bauhaus pin inherited from itten.journey.json
stops.campa: Walter Gropius appoints Klee to the Staatliches Bauhaus on 29 October 1920 and he begins teaching as a Form Master on 10 January 1921. Johannes Itten has been there since October 1919 and has been drawing Swiss and Munich people into the school after him. Klee takes the bookbinding workshop first, then glass painting, and above all the theory of form and colour, which he teaches by drawing on the board and thinking out loud in front of the students. The pedagogy will outlast every building the school ever occupies.
stops.quote: I cannot be grasped in the here and now. For I reside just as much with the dead as with the unborn.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, exhibition catalogue text, Galerie Hans Goltz, Munich, May 1920; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Staatliches Bauhaus Weimar, Form Master appointment, 29 October 1920

stops.name: Weimar, the house on Am Horn
stops.date_confidence: permanent move to Weimar September 1921 attested, day defaulted. The street Am Horn, first number 39 then number 53; not the Haus am Horn, which is the separate 1923 model house
stops.campa: Klee moves his family to Weimar permanently in September 1921 and takes a house on the street Am Horn, first at number 39 and later at number 53, on the slope above the park. Kandinsky joins the faculty in June 1922, and the two men who first shared a classroom under Franz von Stuck are colleagues again twenty-two years later. The Bauhaus holds its first public exhibition in the summer of 1923. Klee's teaching notes from these rooms become the Pedagogical Sketchbook, published as the second Bauhaus book in 1925.
stops.quote: Art does not reproduce the visible; rather, it makes visible.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, 'Creative Credo' (Schopferische Konfession), Section I, 1920; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Am Horn 39 and Am Horn 53, Weimar; the Padagogisches Skizzenbuch, Bauhausbucher 2, 1925

stops.name: Paris, the Surrealists claim him
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Klee's work is shown in Paris for the first time in 1924 and the Surrealists take him up at once as one of their own. Andre Breton renames a 1912 painting to suit his own argument; Max Ernst admires him without reservation and goes on doing so long after Breton has cooled. Klee joins nothing. The year before he had formed Die Blaue Vier with Kandinsky, Feininger, and Jawlensky, a four-man front for exhibitions in America. He is claimed from both sides of the Rhine.
stops.quote: It is interesting to observe how real the object remains, in spite of all abstractions.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, statement, mid-1920s; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The 1924 Paris exhibition; Die Blaue Vier, formed 1923

stops.name: Dessau, the Meisterhaus beside Kandinsky
stops.date_confidence: Klee occupies the Meisterhaus July 1926, day defaulted. The Bauhaus as an institution moved to Dessau in 1925, not 1926; coordinate corrected to the Ebertallee Meisterhauser
stops.campa: The Bauhaus moved to Dessau in 1925; in July 1926 Klee occupies half of a white semi-detached masters' house on the Ebertallee, designed by Gropius, sharing the building with Kandinsky. The new school building opens on 4 December. The two families live wall to wall for five years, Klee painting upstairs to gramophone records of Mozart and Bach, Lily teaching piano downstairs, Felix working in the Bauhaus theatre. The family stays on the Ebertallee until Klee leaves for Düsseldorf in 1931.
stops.quote: The father of the arrow is the thought: how do I expand my reach?
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, Pedagogical Sketchbook, 1925, section IIII.37 'The Arrow', p. 54, in the Sibyl Moholy-Nagy translation (Polyglot Press / Frederick A. Praeger, New York, 1953); via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Meisterhauser Dessau, Ebertallee 69/71, Gropius, 1925-1926

stops.name: Alexandria, the Egyptian journey
stops.date_confidence: 17 December 1928 is the departure date of the whole journey, not the day of arrival at Alexandria, which came some days later; the trip closes 17 January 1929
stops.campa: On 17 December 1928 Klee sets out for Egypt, paid for in part by the collectors of his Kunstverein circle, and comes in by sea to Alexandria. It is his second journey into North African light, fourteen years after Tunisia, and this time he travels comfortably, a famous man on a subsidised tour rather than a hungry one sharing a doctor's spare room. The difference shows in the results. No sentence comes out of Egypt, and no conversion. The horizontal band of colour does, and it runs through the paintings of 1929.
suggested_refs: The Egyptian journey, 17 December 1928 to 17 January 1929

stops.name: Cairo, the pyramid field at Giza
stops.date_confidence: December 1928 attested; the specific day within the journey is reconstructed
stops.campa: Cairo, the museum, and the pyramid field at Giza, where the monuments are too large and too finished to argue with. Klee looks at them the way a man looks at a mountain range. His biographers and he himself agree that Egypt moves him less than Tunisia did: the scale registers as spectacle where Kairouan registered as a lesson. He goes up the Nile to Luxor and Karnak and on as far as Aswan before turning back, reaching home on 17 January 1929. The Egyptian pictures come out as striated fields, stacked like courses of stone.
suggested_refs: Giza, Luxor, Karnak, and Aswan on the 1928-1929 Egyptian itinerary; the 'Hauptweg und Nebenwege' register paintings of 1929

stops.name: Düsseldorf, the Academy chair
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Klee leaves the Bauhaus and takes a professorship at the Düsseldorf Academy from 1 July 1931, keeping the Dessau house and commuting between the two cities. He teaches a painting class with no fixed curriculum and an unusual amount of patience. In Dessau the Nazi-controlled council closes the Bauhaus in 1932; it staggers on in Berlin for a year and then stops for good. Kandinsky, writing as the colleague of eleven years departs, describes what Klee had been in that school in terms nobody at the time thought excessive.
stops.quote: At the Bauhaus, Klee exuded a healthy, generative atmosphere, as a great artist and as a lucid, pure human being.
stops.quote_source: Wassily Kandinsky, in Bauhaus. Zeitschrift fur Gestaltung, 1931; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Kunstakademie Dusseldorf, Klee's painting class, 1931-1933

stops.name: Dessau, the search and the self-portrait
stops.date_confidence: spring 1933, day defaulted; dismissal confirmed 21 April 1933. The house searched was in Dessau, not Dusseldorf as some compilations state
stops.campa: In the spring of 1933 the Nazi press attacks Klee as a Galician Jew passing himself off as an Arab, the Gestapo searches his house in Dessau, and Düsseldorf suspends him; the dismissal is confirmed on 21 April. He is asked to produce proof of Aryan descent. That year he paints a self-portrait and calls it Von der Liste gestrichen, Struck from the List: a flat grey head, eyes shut, mouth a single stitched line, the face of a man whose name has been taken off a register by somebody he will never meet.
stops.quote: Then that great fellow Klee comes onto the scene, already famed as a Bauhaus teacher...He tells everyone he's a thoroughbred Arab, but he's a typical Galician Jew.
stops.quote_source: Nazi press attack on Klee, 1933, cited secondhand on Wikiquote without a named newspaper. [R]: the primary has not been traced.
suggested_refs: 'Von der Liste gestrichen', 1933, Zentrum Paul Klee, Bern

stops.name: Bern, the return to the parents' house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve 1933 Klee crosses into Switzerland for good and moves back into his father's house in Bern, the city he spent his youth getting out of. He is fifty-four, without a post and without a German market, and he has spent the year declining to supply the proof of descent the authorities asked him for. Switzerland is not eager to have him either: the naturalisation office files him as a foreign artist of doubtful tendency and takes six years over his application. The exile is comfortable and total.
stops.quote: I'll provide it if I'm officially asked to do so but it's below my dignity to initiate action against such primitive accusations.
stops.quote_source: Paul Klee, letter to Lily Klee, 6 April 1933, on the demand for proof of Aryan descent; via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Klee family house in Bern, Obstbergweg 6

stops.name: Bern, Kistlerweg 6
stops.date_confidence: June 1934 attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: From June 1934 Klee and Lily rent a three-room apartment at Kistlerweg 6 in the Elfenau quarter, and he works in a room hardly wider than a corridor. He was born in Switzerland but was never Swiss: the citizenship came from his German father, and the Bern authorities are in no hurry to change that. In 1935 the first symptoms appear of the scleroderma that will kill him, a hardening of skin and connective tissue that stiffens the hands and narrows the mouth. In 1936 he manages twenty-five pictures in the whole year.
suggested_refs: Kistlerweg 6, Elfenau, Bern, the Klee apartment from June 1934

stops.name: Munich, the Degenerate Art exhibition
stops.date_confidence: the exhibition opens 19 July 1937; Klee's inclusion and the confiscation figures are attested, the opening day is the exhibition's not a Klee event
stops.campa: On 19 July 1937 the Entartete Kunst exhibition opens in Munich with seventeen works by Klee on its walls, hung crooked and captioned to be laughed at. In the same operation 102 of his works are seized from German public collections. The country that named him a leading figure of its new art in 1917 exhibits him twenty years later as evidence of disease. He is in Bern, ill, and does not see it. What he does that year is paint 264 pictures, the opening of the largest working surge of his life.
suggested_refs: Entartete Kunst, Hofgarten arcades, Munich, 19 July to 30 November 1937

stops.name: Bern, Picasso at the door
stops.date_confidence: late 1937, month and day reconstructed. Some compilations date a Klee and Picasso meeting to 1933; no source reachable here supports that, and the documented encounter is this Bern visit
stops.campa: In late 1937 Pablo Picasso comes to Kistlerweg 6 to see him, an hour of two painters in a small Bern apartment with a sick man's brushes on the table. Georges Braque comes the following year. Klee had gone to look at Picasso at the Kunsthaus Zurich in October 1932; now Picasso comes to look at him. He is fifty-eight, his hands stiffening, and about to produce 489 works in 1938 and 1,254 in 1939, drawing with a thick black line because a thick black line is what the disease still permits him.
suggested_refs: Picasso's visit to Kistlerweg 6, Bern, late 1937

stops.name: Muralto, the Clinica Sant'Agnese
stops.date_confidence: attested; admitted 10 May 1940
stops.campa: On 10 May 1940 Klee is taken south to the Ticino and admitted to the Clinica Sant'Agnese at Muralto beside Lake Maggiore. He dies there on 29 June, aged sixty, of heart failure brought on by the scleroderma. In his last months he has drawn some fifty angels and painted Tod und Feuer, in which the German word for death is built into the bones of a face. His naturalisation was approved on 19 December 1939; the citizenship itself is conferred six days after he stops needing it.
suggested_refs: 'Tod und Feuer', 1940, Zentrum Paul Klee; the angel drawings of 1939-1940

stops.name: Bern, the Schosshaldenfriedhof
stops.date_confidence: July 1940, day defaulted; coordinate corrected, the research pool carried two different and both wrong positions for this cemetery
stops.campa: Klee is buried at the Schosshaldenfriedhof on the eastern edge of Bern. His son Felix chooses the words for the bronze plate, taking them from the catalogue text his father wrote for Hans Goltz twenty years earlier. The man under the stone was a German citizen born in Switzerland. He worked in Germany until Germany expelled him in 1933, and he was still a German citizen when he died. Bern conferred Swiss citizenship on the fifth of July, six days later.
stops.quote: I cannot be grasped in the here and now, for my dwelling place is as much among the dead as the yet unborn. Slightly closer to the heart of creation than usual, but still not close enough.
stops.quote_source: Epitaph on Klee's grave, Schosshaldenfriedhof, Bern, chosen by Felix Klee from the 1920 Goltz catalogue text
suggested_refs: The Klee grave, Schosshaldenfriedhof, Bern

stops.name: Paris, the Angelus Novus left behind
stops.date_confidence: Benjamin leaves Paris in June 1940, day defaulted. Canonical atlas Paris pin inherited from the existing corpus
stops.campa: Walter Benjamin bought Klee's oil-transfer monoprint Angelus Novus in 1921 and hung it in every room he lived in afterwards. He carried it into exile in 1933. In 1940, leaving Paris ahead of the Wehrmacht, he left it with Georges Bataille, who hid it in the Bibliotheque Nationale; from there it reached Theodor Adorno and then Gershom Scholem, as Benjamin's instructions required. Benjamin died at Portbou in September. Klee had died in June. Neither man learned of the other's death, and the angel outlived them both.
stops.quote: This storm is what we call progress.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'Theses on the Philosophy of History', 1940, on Klee's Angelus Novus; via Wikipedia, 'Angelus Novus'
suggested_refs: Walter Benjamin, 'Uber den Begriff der Geschichte', thesis IX, 1940

stops.name: Bern, the Zentrum Paul Klee
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate corrected, the research pool's value fell about 1.1 km away
stops.campa: In 1997 Livia Klee-Meyer, the artist's daughter-in-law, gives some 690 works to the city and canton of Bern. On 20 June 2005 the Zentrum Paul Klee opens on the Schongrun site east of the city: three steel hills by Renzo Piano rolling up out of a field, a museum built in the shape of landscape. It holds roughly four thousand works, about forty percent of everything Klee made, and can show almost none of it at a time, because the inks and watercolours he worked in go pale in daylight. The collection lives in the dark.
stops.quote: In any painting or drawing by Klee the working method was broadly the same. He started every picture with an abstract mark...and then allowed that motif to evolve.
stops.quote_source: Richard Dorment, review of the Tate Modern exhibition, The Telegraph, 14 October 2013. [R]: a critic's own formulation, secondary, not a Klee statement.
suggested_refs: Zentrum Paul Klee, Monument im Fruchtland 3, Bern, Renzo Piano, opened 20 June 2005

stops.name: Jerusalem, the angel in the Israel Museum
stops.date_confidence: the Quaytman discovery is dated 2015; month and day defaulted. Museum coordinate, deliberately not the corpus Temple Mount pin
stops.campa: Angelus Novus hangs in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, a small brown angel that a philosopher turned into the angel of history and that has been read ever since as a picture about catastrophe. In 2015 the artist R. H. Quaytman examines the sheet and finds that Klee pasted it over a reused copperplate engraving of Martin Luther, printed in 1838, hidden under the image for almost a century. The picture has a second face on its back, and Klee left no note about it.
suggested_refs: Angelus Novus, 1920, Israel Museum, Jerusalem; R. H. Quaytman's 2015 examination of the substrate
